reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / WHO Classification of Skin Tumours
clinicalPearls: A benign adnexal tumour of eccrine sweat-duct differentiation, presenting as small skin-coloured to yellowish papules
Most characteristically clustered symmetrically on the lower eyelids and periorbital skin, more common in women
Eruptive syringomas can appear in crops on the trunk, and there is an association with Down syndrome
Lesions are usually asymptomatic and stable, sought mainly for cosmetic reasons rather than medical concern
Histology shows small ducts lined by two layers of epithelial cells, some with a comma-like or tadpole tail, embedded in a sclerotic dermal stroma
The tadpole/comma-shaped ducts distinguish syringoma from other basaloid adnexal tumours
Treatment is optional and cosmetic; options include ablative or destructive methods, with recurrence common because lesions are numerous
reference.pathophysiology: Syringoma is a benign adnexal neoplasm derived from the intraepidermal portion of the eccrine sweat duct. Histologically it consists of numerous small ducts and solid epithelial strands set within a fibrous, often sclerotic, dermal stroma; the ducts are lined by two layers of cuboidal cells and many acquire a characteristic comma-like or tadpole configuration. The lesions represent a proliferation of well-differentiated ductal structures rather than an aggressive process, so they remain confined to the dermis without invasion or metastatic potential. Hormonal and genetic influences are thought to contribute, reflected in the female predominance, the tendency to periorbital clustering, and the eruptive forms associated with certain systemic conditions.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination of the periorbital and eyelid skin for characteristic clustered papules
Skin biopsy with histopathology showing tadpole-shaped ducts in sclerotic stroma
Dermoscopy to help distinguish from xanthelasma and other papules
Immunohistochemistry in equivocal cases to distinguish from microcystic adnexal carcinoma
Assessment for associated conditions when lesions are eruptive or widespread
redFlags: An indurated infiltrative plaque rather than discrete papules, raising concern for microcystic adnexal carcinoma
Rapid change or ulceration atypical for benign syringoma
Widespread eruptive lesions prompting evaluation for an associated systemic condition
reference.prognosis: Syringomas are entirely benign with no malignant potential; they are cosmetically bothersome and tend to persist, and treatment can be complicated by recurrence and scarring given the number and depth of lesions.
pitfalls: Confusing periorbital syringomas with xanthelasma and pursuing lipid-lowering rather than dermatological assessment
Misinterpreting the sclerotic ductal histology as microcystic adnexal carcinoma or morphoeic basal cell carcinoma
Promising complete cosmetic clearance despite a high recurrence rate
Overlooking the association with systemic conditions in eruptive presentations
management: Syringoma is a benign eccrine adnexal tumour, so treatment is elective and cosmetic rather than disease directed, with no stage or intent based systemic therapy pathway
Asymptomatic, stable, cosmetically acceptable lesions can simply be observed with reassurance, no treatment is medically required

Cosmetically bothersome periorbital or clustered lesions are managed with destructive or ablative modalities such as ablative laser resurfacing, electrodesiccation or electrocautery, dermabrasion, or chemical destruction with trichloroacetic acid
Isolated or few papules can be treated with surgical excision or focal cautery, though excising every lesion in an eruptive or densely clustered case is impractical and scar prone

Eruptive or widespread syringomatosis should prompt work-up for an associated systemic condition, such as Down syndrome or a metabolic or endocrine trigger, rather than escalating local destructive therapy
There is no first-line or second-line systemic therapy ladder, sequencing is escalation of cosmetic intervention from observation to destructive treatment to repeat treatment for recurrence

Surgery is limited to excising an individual troublesome papule or obtaining a biopsy before destructive treatment when a lesion looks atypical, it is not used as definitive therapy for numerous lesions
Radiotherapy and systemic therapy including chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy have no established role in benign syringoma

Follow-up is driven by cosmetic goals and recurrence rather than oncologic surveillance, and recurrence after destructive treatment is common so patients should be counselled that repeat sessions are often needed

Any lesion that becomes indurated, infiltrative, rapidly enlarging, or ulcerated should prompt re-biopsy rather than repeat cosmetic treatment, to exclude a malignant mimic such as microcystic adnexal carcinoma, morpheaform basal cell carcinoma, or desmoplastic trichoepithelioma
Refer to dermatology, or ophthalmology for periorbital lesions, for diagnostic confirmation and destructive or ablative cosmetic treatment
Refer for repeat biopsy and to a specialist familiar with adnexal tumour pathology whenever a lesion behaves atypically, so a malignant mimic is not treated and destroyed like a benign syringoma
Refer for genetics, paediatric, or endocrine assessment when syringomas are eruptive and widespread and an associated systemic condition is suspected but not yet established
